0.title: The Law of Love for the People of Grace
0.overview:
The Ten Commandments are among the most famous words ever spoken. For centuries they shaped the laws and morals of nations. Children memorised them, and churches displayed them on their walls. Today many people know little about them, and many Christians are unsure how they apply. Are they still binding? Were they only for Israel? Does grace make the law irrelevant?

The Bible's answer is rich. The commandments begin not with a demand but with a reminder of grace: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Exod 20:2). God rescued his people first, then gave them his law. The law was never a ladder to climb up to God. It was a way of life for those he had already redeemed.

Jesus summed up the law in two great commandments: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself (Matt 22:37-39). The Ten Commandments fall into those two tables: the first four about love for God, the last six about love for neighbour. And Jesus showed that each reaches the heart, not only outward behaviour.

Six units: (1) The Law and the Christian; (2) No Other Gods, No Images; (3) God's Name and God's Day; (4) Honour and Life; (5) Faithfulness and Property; (6) Truth, Contentment and the Law Fulfilled.

1.title: The Law and the Christian
1.overview:
Grace before law. God spoke the Ten Commandments to Israel at Sinai after he had rescued them from Egypt. The order is crucial. Obedience is not the way to become God's people; it is the response of those who already are. The same is true for Christians. We are saved by grace through faith, not by keeping the law (Eph 2:8-9). But saved people are called to live God's way.

The law is good. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (Rom 7:12). The law reflects God's own character. It is not arbitrary. It describes what love looks like: love for God and love for others. Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day (Ps 119:97).

The law shows our sin. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom 3:20). The law is like a mirror. It shows us our true condition, and drives us to Christ. Paul says he would not have known what coveting was without the commandment (Rom 7:7).

Christ fulfils the law. Jesus said, Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them (Matt 5:17). He kept the law perfectly in our place. He bore the curse of the law for our sins (Gal 3:13). And he fulfils the law in us by his Spirit, writing it on our hearts (Jer 31:33; Rom 8:4).

Jesus deepens the law. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus showed that the commandments reach the heart. Anger is the root of murder. Lust is adultery in the heart. The law is not satisfied with outward conformity. It calls for a pure heart, which only the Spirit can give.
1.theology:
Three uses of the law: The Reformed tradition speaks of three uses. First, the law restrains evil in society. Second, it shows sinners their need and drives them to Christ. Third, it guides believers in how to live in gratitude. Christians are not under the law as a way of salvation, but they delight in it as a guide.

Moral, ceremonial and civil law: The law of Moses included moral laws (such as the Ten Commandments), ceremonial laws (sacrifices, food laws, festivals) and civil laws for Israel as a nation. The ceremonial laws were fulfilled in Christ and are no longer binding (Heb 10:1; Col 2:16-17). The civil laws expired with Israel as a nation, though their justice still instructs. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflects God's unchanging character and continues to guide Christians.

Legalism and lawlessness: Two errors threaten the Christian life. Legalism tries to earn God's favour by keeping rules, or adds human rules to God's law. Lawlessness (antinomianism) says grace means the law no longer matters. Scripture rejects both. Grace saves us and then teaches us to obey (Titus 2:11-12).
1.examples:
Then: When the rich young ruler asked what he must do to inherit eternal life, Jesus listed several commandments. The man said he had kept them all since his youth. Jesus then said, go, sell all that you have (Mark 10:21). The young man went away sorrowful. The law exposed the idol he loved more than God.

Now: A new Christian thinks the Ten Commandments belong to the Old Testament and have nothing to do with her. Studying them, she discovers that they describe the life Jesus lived and the life the Spirit is producing in her. She begins to read them as a portrait of love, not a list of restrictions.

A simple test: Do you see God's law as a burden, a ladder or a guide? Psalm 119 sees it as a delight.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke all these words, saying, "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Before a single command is given, God identifies himself: the LORD your God, your rescuer. The commandments are spoken to a redeemed people. Every command that follows should be read in that light. God is not a tyrant laying down rules for slaves. He is a Saviour describing life in freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it. Not the smallest letter will pass away until all is accomplished. Then he says something shocking: our righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. Their righteousness was outward. Jesus calls for a righteousness of the heart, which only he can give.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead. I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me. For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul explains that the law is not sin. Rather, it exposes sin. The commandment against coveting made him aware of covetousness in his heart. Sin used the commandment to bring death. Yet the law itself is holy, righteous and good. The problem is not the law, but us.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him. "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?" And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A lawyer asked Jesus which commandment is the greatest. Jesus answered with two: love God with all your heart, soul and mind, and love your neighbour as yourself. All the Law and the Prophets depend on these two. The Ten Commandments are love spelled out.

1.reflection:
Why is it important that the commandments begin with God's rescue from Egypt?

What are the three uses of the law? Which do you most need?

How does Jesus deepen the commandments in the Sermon on the Mount?

Do you lean more toward legalism or lawlessness? How does the gospel correct you?

2.title: No Other Gods, No Images
2.overview:
The first commandment: no other gods. You shall have no other gods before me (Exod 20:3). The first commandment is first because everything depends on it. God alone is to be worshipped, trusted, loved and obeyed. Israel was surrounded by nations with many gods. God's people were to have one.

Modern idols. Few people today bow to statues, but idolatry is everywhere. An idol is anything we trust, love or fear more than God: money, career, comfort, reputation, relationships, pleasure or even family. Paul calls covetousness idolatry (Col 3:5). The question is not whether we worship, but what. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:21).

The positive command. The first commandment calls us to love God wholeheartedly: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might (Deut 6:4-5).

The second commandment: no images. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them (Exod 20:4-5). The first commandment governs whom we worship; the second governs how. God may not be represented by images, because no image can capture him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4:24).

The golden calf. When Israel made the golden calf, Aaron declared a feast to the LORD (Exod 32:5). They thought they were worshipping the true God through an image. God called it idolatry. Images reduce God to something we can see, control and shape according to our own ideas.

A jealous God. God attaches a warning and a promise: he is a jealous God, but he shows steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments (Exod 20:5-6). His jealousy is the right jealousy of a husband for his wife. And his love far outweighs his judgment.
2.theology:
Worshipping God his way: The second commandment underlies the Reformed regulative principle: God must be worshipped as he has commanded, not according to human invention. The Worship and the Lord's Day study explores this further.

Pictures of Jesus: the views. Some Reformed Christians hold that the second commandment forbids any picture of Christ, since he is God and no image can represent his divine nature. Others hold that since the Son became visible man, depicting his humanity for teaching is permissible, provided images are never used in worship.

The verdict: Images must never be used as aids to worship, prayed to or venerated. Beyond that, Christians should be very cautious. Any picture of Jesus is imagined, and it can shape and limit how we think of him. Scripture gives us no description of his appearance, perhaps deliberately. We know him through the word.
2.examples:
Then: Elijah challenged the people of Israel on Mount Carmel: How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him (1 Kgs 18:21). Israel wanted both. The first commandment does not allow divided loyalty.

Now: A Christian man realises that his anxiety about money reveals that he trusts his savings more than God. He has never bowed to a statue, but money has become his functional god. He confesses this as idolatry, begins giving generously and learns to trust God for the future.

A simple test: What do you think about most, fear losing most and turn to for comfort? That may be your idol.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall have no other gods before me. "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first two commandments guard the heart of worship. No other gods, and no images. God's jealousy is not petty but protective. He will not share his glory with idols that destroy his people. And his covenant love reaches to thousands of generations, far beyond his judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might. And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. You shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. You shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Shema, Israel's great confession, declares that the LORD is one and calls for wholehearted love. These words were to be on the heart, taught to children, spoken at home and on the road, bound on hands and written on doorposts. Love for God shapes all of life.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron and said to him, "Up, make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him." So Aaron said to them, "Take off the rings of gold that are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me." So all the people took off the rings of gold that were in their ears and brought them to Aaron. And he received the gold from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made a golden calf. And they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it. And Aaron made a proclamation and said, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD." And they rose up early the next day and offered burnt offerings and brought peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: While Moses was on the mountain, the people demanded gods to go before them. Aaron made a golden calf and called it the god who brought them out of Egypt. They thought they were worshipping the LORD. God saw it as breaking both the first and second commandments, within weeks of hearing them.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John ends his letter by declaring that the Son of God has come and given us understanding to know the true God. Jesus Christ is the true God and eternal life. Then the final command: keep yourselves from idols. Knowing the true God is the best protection against false ones.

2.reflection:
What are the most common idols in your culture? In your own heart?

Why does God forbid images in worship?

Read Exodus 32. How did Israel break the first two commandments while thinking they were worshipping God?

What would it mean to love God with all your heart, soul and might this week?

3.title: God's Name and God's Day
3.overview:
The third commandment: God's name. You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain (Exod 20:7). God's name represents his character and reputation. To take it in vain means to treat it as empty or worthless.

Ways we misuse God's name. The most obvious is using it as a swear word or casual exclamation. But the commandment goes further. It is broken by false oaths made in God's name, by claiming God's authority for our own ideas ("God told me..."), by careless or irreverent speech about God and by hypocrisy, when people who bear his name live in ways that dishonour him (Rom 2:24).

The positive command. The first petition of the Lord's Prayer is the positive side of this commandment: Hallowed be your name (Matt 6:9). We are to speak of God with reverence, praise his name and live so that others honour it.

The fourth commandment: the Sabbath. Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God (Exod 20:8-10). The Sabbath was rooted in creation, as God rested on the seventh day, and in redemption, as Israel was freed from slavery (Deut 5:15). It was a weekly reminder that life depends on God, not on our labour.

Fulfilled in Christ. Jesus is lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28) and offers true rest to the weary (Matt 11:28). Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow, of which Christ is the substance (Col 2:16-17). Christians enter God's rest by faith in Christ (Heb 4:9-10). The weekly Sabbath law is fulfilled in him.

The Lord's Day and rest. The early church gathered on the first day, the day of resurrection (Acts 20:7; Rev 1:10). Gathering with God's people on the Lord's Day is a clear apostolic pattern. And the rhythm of rest God built into creation remains wise and good. We are not machines. Regular rest is an act of trust in God.
3.theology:
The fourth commandment: the views. Many Reformed Christians hold that the fourth commandment remains a moral law, with Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, kept by rest from ordinary work and recreation. Others hold that the Sabbath command was part of Israel's covenant sign (Exod 31:13), fulfilled in Christ.

The verdict: The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, as Colossians 2:16-17 and Romans 14:5-6 show. Yet the principle of rest and the gathering of the church on the Lord's Day remain. Christians who differ on this should not judge one another (Rom 14:4-6). The Worship and the Lord's Day study treats this more fully.

Oaths: Jesus said, Do not take an oath at all, but let your yes be yes (Matt 5:34-37). Most Christians have understood this as forbidding casual or manipulative oaths, not solemn oaths in court, since God himself swore by himself (Heb 6:13).
3.examples:
Then: In Leviticus, a man in a fight blasphemed the Name of the LORD and cursed. He was brought to Moses, and God commanded that he be put to death (Lev 24:10-16). In Israel, God's name was so sacred that misusing it was a capital offence.

Now: A young man has always used "Oh my God" as a casual exclamation, without thinking. After studying the third commandment, he becomes aware of it and decides to stop. He finds that his reverence for God grows when he guards his speech about God.

A simple test: Do you speak of God casually or reverently? Do you ever claim his authority for your own opinions?

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The third and fourth commandments protect God's name and God's time. His name must not be treated as empty. One day in seven was to be set apart, with rest extended to everyone in the household, including servants, foreigners and animals. Both commandments call for reverence and trust.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray then like this: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Lord's Prayer begins not with our needs but with God's name, kingdom and will. Hallowed be your name is the third commandment turned into prayer. We ask God to make his name honoured, in our lives and in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, "Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?" And he said to them, "Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?" And he said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: When the Pharisees criticised his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus declared that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. The one who made the Sabbath has authority over it.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his. Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A Sabbath rest remains for God's people. It is entered by ceasing from our own works and trusting Christ, and it will be completed in glory. The weekly Sabbath pointed forward to this rest. Believers are called to strive to enter it.

3.reflection:
In what ways can God's name be "taken in vain" besides swearing?

How can you hallow God's name in your daily life?

How is the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ?

How can you use the Lord's Day for worship and rest?

4.title: Honour and Life
4.overview:
The second table of the law begins with the family and with life itself.

The fifth commandment: honour parents. Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you (Exod 20:12). Paul notes that this is the first commandment with a promise (Eph 6:2). Honour includes obedience for children (Eph 6:1), respect at every age and care for parents in their old age. Jesus rebuked those who used religious excuses to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:9-13).

Wider authority. The fifth commandment also shapes how we relate to other authorities God has established: government, employers, church leaders. Honour does not mean blind obedience; we must obey God rather than men when they conflict (Acts 5:29). But it means respect and appropriate submission.

When parents fail. Some parents are abusive, absent or ungodly. Honouring them does not mean pretending, obeying sinful commands or exposing oneself to harm. It may mean speaking respectfully, praying for them, forgiving them and caring for their needs as far as is wise.

The sixth commandment: do not murder. You shall not murder (Exod 20:13). Human life is sacred because people are made in God's image (Gen 9:6). This commandment forbids taking innocent life, including abortion, euthanasia and suicide.

Jesus deepens it. You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment." But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment (Matt 5:21-22). Murder begins in the heart, in anger, contempt and hatred. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15).

The positive command. The sixth commandment calls us to protect and preserve life: caring for the sick, defending the vulnerable, making peace and looking after our own health.
4.theology:
Murder and killing: The commandment forbids murder, the unjust taking of human life. Scripture permits the state to execute justice (Rom 13:4) and recognises self-defence (Exod 22:2). Christians have differed on war, capital punishment and pacifism, but all agree that innocent life must be protected.

The unborn: Scripture treats unborn children as persons known by God (Ps 139:13-16; Jer 1:5; Luke 1:41-44). Abortion takes innocent human life. Yet those who have been involved in abortion can find full forgiveness in Christ.

Anger and reconciliation: Right after deepening the sixth commandment, Jesus calls for urgent reconciliation (Matt 5:23-24). Dealing with anger quickly is part of keeping this commandment.
4.examples:
Then: Ruth honoured her mother-in-law Naomi by staying with her and providing for her. Jesus, dying on the cross, made sure his mother would be cared for, entrusting her to John (John 19:26-27). Even in agony, he kept the fifth commandment.

Now: A woman whose elderly father was harsh and critical throughout her childhood struggles to know how to honour him. With counsel, she decides to visit him regularly, care for his practical needs and speak respectfully, while not exposing herself to his verbal abuse. She has forgiven him, though trust has not been fully restored.

A simple test: Is there anger in your heart toward someone that Jesus would call a form of murder?

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. "Honor your father and mother" (this is the first commandment with a promise), "that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land." Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul calls children to obey their parents in the Lord and reminds them of the fifth commandment's promise. Then he calls fathers not to provoke their children to anger, but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Honour flows both ways in a Christian home.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother'; and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.' But you say, 'If a man tells his father or his mother, "Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban"' (that is, given to God) — then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees had a tradition that allowed people to declare their money "Corban," given to God, and so avoid supporting their parents. Jesus condemned this as making void the word of God. Religion can never be an excuse for neglecting family duty.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.' But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, 'You fool!' will be liable to the hell of fire. So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus takes the sixth commandment to the heart. Anger, insults and contempt make us liable to judgment. Then he gives urgent instructions: leave your gift at the altar and be reconciled; settle with your accuser quickly. Anger must be dealt with before it grows.

verseByVerse.quote: And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man. "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After the flood, God established the sanctity of human life. Whoever sheds human blood will be held accountable, because God made man in his own image. Every human life bears God's image, which is why it is sacred.

4.reflection:
How can you honour your parents, whatever your age or their character?

Why does Jesus connect anger and contempt with murder?

How does the image of God shape your view of human life?

Is there someone you need to be reconciled with this week?

5.title: Faithfulness and Property
5.overview:
The seventh commandment: do not commit adultery. You shall not commit adultery (Exod 20:14). Marriage is a covenant between one man and one woman for life, and sexual union belongs within it. Adultery betrays a spouse, breaks a covenant and harms children and families.

Jesus deepens it. But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28). The seventh commandment covers lust, pornography and all sexual immorality, in thought, word and deed. It also calls for positive faithfulness: cherishing one's spouse and guarding one's heart.

Hope for the guilty. David committed adultery and was forgiven when he repented (Ps 51). Jesus forgave sexual sinners and called them to new life. No sexual sin is beyond the reach of grace. The Biblical Sexuality study treats this commandment more fully.

The eighth commandment: do not steal. You shall not steal (Exod 20:15). Stealing is taking what belongs to another. It includes obvious theft, but also fraud, cheating on taxes, wasting an employer's time, failing to pay debts, plagiarism and exploiting workers with unjust wages (Jas 5:4).

The positive command. Paul gives the alternative: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need (Eph 4:28). The cure for stealing is not only stopping, but working and giving. The eighth commandment calls for honest work and generosity.

Robbing God. Malachi asked, Will man rob God? The people had withheld their tithes and contributions (Mal 3:8). Our possessions belong ultimately to God, and we are stewards.
5.theology:
Property and stewardship: The eighth commandment assumes that people may rightly own property. Yet Scripture also teaches that everything belongs to God (Ps 24:1). We are stewards, not absolute owners, and we are called to use our resources for God's glory and others' good.

Restitution: In the Old Testament, thieves were required to repay, often several times over (Exod 22:1). Zacchaeus, when he came to Christ, promised to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated (Luke 19:8). Repentance for theft includes making things right where possible.

Faithfulness in all of life: The seventh and eighth commandments both concern faithfulness: to our spouse and to what belongs to others. Both protect relationships of trust.
5.examples:
Then: Achan, during the conquest of Jericho, stole silver, gold and a cloak that were devoted to God, and hid them in his tent. His sin brought defeat on all Israel (Josh 7). Hidden theft has public consequences.

Now: A Christian employee realises she has been spending an hour a day on personal browsing at work. She sees this as stealing from her employer. She confesses it to God, changes her habits and works with new diligence. Her manager notices and later promotes her.

A simple test: Is there anything in your life, at work, at home or online, that amounts to stealing or unfaithfulness?

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus takes the seventh commandment to the heart. Lustful looking is adultery of the heart. Then he calls for radical action: cut off whatever causes you to sin. The seventh commandment is kept not only by avoiding the act, but by guarding the eyes and the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched? So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife; none who touches her will go unpunished. People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry, but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house. He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself. He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs warns that adultery is like carrying fire in one's lap. A thief who steals because he is hungry may be pitied, though he must repay. But the adulterer destroys himself, and his disgrace will not be wiped away. The seventh and eighth commandments are compared and contrasted here.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The former thief is not only to stop stealing. He is to work honestly, so that he can share with those in need. The gospel turns a taker into a giver. This is the positive heart of the eighth commandment.

verseByVerse.quote: Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Agur prays for two things: keep falsehood far from me, and give me neither poverty nor riches. If he is rich, he might deny God; if poor, he might steal and profane God's name. A contented heart is the best protection against stealing.

5.reflection:
How does Jesus deepen the seventh commandment?

In what subtle ways might you be breaking the eighth commandment?

How does Ephesians 4:28 show the positive side of the eighth commandment?

How can you guard your heart and eyes this week?

6.title: Truth, Contentment and the Law Fulfilled
6.overview:
The ninth commandment: do not bear false witness. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor (Exod 20:16). The commandment originally concerned testimony in court, where lies could destroy a person. But it reaches all our speech: lying, slander, gossip, flattery and deception. It also calls us to speak truth, to defend the reputation of others and to keep our promises. The Tongue study treats this more fully.

The tenth commandment: do not covet. You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's (Exod 20:17). The last commandment reaches into the heart. Coveting is an inner desire, invisible to others. It shows that God's law is not only about actions but about desires. Coveting is often the root of breaking the other commandments: stealing, adultery and lying.

Contentment. The opposite of coveting is contentment: be content with what you have, for he has said, "I will never leave you nor forsake you." (Heb 13:5). Contentment rests on God's presence, not our possessions.

Love fulfils the law. Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." (Rom 13:8-9). Love is not a replacement for the commandments. It is their fulfilment.

The law written on the heart. In the new covenant, God promised, I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33). What the stone tablets could not achieve, the Spirit accomplishes. The law that once condemned us now describes the life the Spirit is producing in us.

Christ, the law-keeper. Only one person has ever kept the Ten Commandments perfectly: Jesus Christ. He loved God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself. His perfect obedience is credited to all who trust him. And by his Spirit, he is making them like himself.
6.theology:
The law cannot save: No one is justified by keeping the law (Gal 2:16). Every commandment, honestly examined, convicts us. That is one of its purposes: to drive us to Christ. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith (Gal 3:24).

The law guides the saved: Once justified by faith, believers delight in God's law as a guide for grateful living. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome (1 John 5:3).

Fulfilled by the Spirit: God sent his Son in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit (Rom 8:4). The law is fulfilled in believers not by their own strength but by the Spirit's work.
6.examples:
Then: Ahab coveted Naboth's vineyard. His wife Jezebel arranged for false witnesses to accuse Naboth, who was then stoned to death, and Ahab took the vineyard (1 Kgs 21). Coveting led to false witness, murder and theft. The commandments stand or fall together.

Now: A Christian reads through the Ten Commandments slowly, asking how he has broken each one in thought, word and deed. By the end, he is humbled, seeing that he has broken them all in his heart. Then he reads Romans 8:1, There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. He has never been so grateful for the gospel, or so eager to obey.

A simple test: Read through the Ten Commandments and ask how each one applies to your heart. Then thank God for Christ, who kept them for you.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. "You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The last two commandments guard truth and the heart. False witness destroys reputations and justice. Coveting desires what belongs to others. The tenth commandment shows that the whole law is ultimately about the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul summarises the second table of the law in one word: love your neighbour as yourself. Love does no wrong to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law. The commandments are not abolished by love; they are the shape that love takes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke, though I was their husband, declares the LORD. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, 'Know the LORD,' for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God promised a new covenant, unlike the one Israel broke. He would put his law within them and write it on their hearts. All would know him, and he would forgive their sin. This promise is fulfilled in Christ and the gift of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death. For God has done what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do. By sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, in order that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: There is no condemnation for those in Christ. The law could not save because of the weakness of our flesh. So God sent his Son to condemn sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. The law's goal is reached through the gospel.

6.reflection:
How is coveting often the root of breaking other commandments?

Read Romans 13:8-10. How does love fulfil the law?

What does it mean to have God's law written on your heart?

Read through all Ten Commandments slowly. Which convicts you most? Thank God for Christ's perfect obedience.
